To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there is a good linear correlation between plasma cholesterol and vitamin E and vitamin K1, and that the correlations are independent of the presence of other risk factors for cardiovascular diseases.

vitamin K1 and vitamin E are positively associated with serum cholesterol concentrations, and that these associations are stronger than the associations between cholesterol and established risk factors for cardiovascular diseases.

(a) the concentrations of vitamins E and of K1 are positively correlated with the plasma concentrations of cholesterol and of low-density lipoprotein; (b) the concentrations of vitamin E are negatively correlated with those of triglycerides; (c) the concentrations of cholesterol and triglycerides are negatively correlated with each other; and (d) the concentrations of the two vitamins and of the two lipids are positively correlated with each other.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a paradoxical relationship between cholesterol, vitamins E and K, and cardiovascular disease.
the relationships of cholesterol, vitamin E and vitamin K1 to established epidemiological and biochemical risk factors for atherosclerosis.
the paradoxical relationship between vitamins K1, E, and cholesterol.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the paradoxical relationships between vitamins K1 and vitamin E, and plasma cholesterol concentrations are not atherogenic.
the epidemiological and clinical data on vitamins E and K do not support the hypothesis that these vitamins are antiatherosclerotic.
the relationship of vitamin K1 to atherogenesis is not clear, but that the relationship of the vitamin E to atherogenesis has not been clarified.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the paradoxical relationships between cholesterol, vitamin K1, and vitamin E in plasma may have to be explained by a more complex relationship between the three compounds than the linear correlations suggest.
the epidemiological and the biochemical viewpoints are not mutually exclusive, and both are valid.
vitamin K1, which is the most atherogenic of the two vitamins, is the most antiatherogenic.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the relationship between cholesterol and the fat-soluble vitamin concentrations is not a linear one.
the relationship of cholesterol with vitamins E and K in serum is a complex one, which cannot be explained by a single factor.

the paradox can be explained if the atherogenicity of cholesterol is considered as a function of the ratio of cholesterol to phospholipid (PC + SM) rather than as an absolute concentration of cholesterol.
